title: client-probe-scheduling-and-batching-design-notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note exploring a client-side probing/scheduling approach for throughput benchmarking that reduces noise from *client pacing* and *thermal/batching coupling*. Goal is a small, implementable harness pattern that keeps runs reproducible across labs and cloud providers.

Background / motivation:
- We repeatedly see variability in throughput runs caused by: client timers drifting, concurrent priming traffic, and server-side batching dynamics coupling to client inter-arrival behavior.
- Existing runbooks focus on warmup length and RNG seeds; this doc focuses on the *probe schedule* (how clients send) and quick mitigations for thermal and batch-related drift.
- Intended audience: bench authors, SREs running infra experiments, and solutions engineers validating customer SLAs.

Definitions (how I use terms here):
- probe: a single request from a synthetic client (may be multi-turn or streaming).
- cohort: a group of probes tied to the same client id / KV-cache affinity.
- sweep: a continuous sequence of probes used to collect steady-state stats.
- microburst: a short duration (~100ms-2s) increase in QPS from a subset of clients.
- occupancy: average in-flight token count across GPUs in the serving cluster.

Design constraints and objectives:
- Minimize correlations between client scheduler jitter and server batching windows.
- Preserve realistic arrival patterns (we still want spike/mix tests) but isolate steady throughput measurements from priming artifacts.
- Keep harness simple to run in CI and in lab: config should be a small YAML/JSON blob.

High-level approach:
1) Split test into phases: L0 (seed priming), L1 (probe-stabilize), L2 (steady sweep), L3 (cooldown capture).
2) Use an anti-synchronization jitter schedule per client: deterministic but different offsets per client derived from a config seed.
3) Maintain cohort affinity for a configurable fraction of requests to exercise KV cache without causing global priming storms.
4) Sample batch windows via low-overhead observability hooks (batch size histograms, GPU occupancy, kernel time).

Sample loadbench config (pseudo-yaml, drop into loadbench v3):

---
clients: 128
concurrency_per_client: 1
target_qps: 3200
phases:
  - name: seed-priming
    duration_s: 300
    pattern: ramp
    ramp_to_qps: 3200
    cohort_affinity_pct: 0.35
  - name: probe-stabilize
    duration_s: 120
    pattern: jittered-interval
    base_interval_ms: 40
    jitter_seed: 12345
  - name: steady-sweep
    duration_s: 1800
    pattern: jittered-interval
    base_interval_ms: 40
    jitter_seed: 12345
    collect_metrics: [latency_p50,latency_p99,qps,batch_size_hist,kv_hit_rate,gpu_occupancy]
  - name: cooldown
    duration_s: 60
    pattern: linear-decrease

notes:
- jittered-interval: algorithm described below; deterministic per-client offsets to avoid bulk alignment.
- cohort_affinity_pct: fraction of requests that reuse the same client id / conversation id to exercise in-memory KV caching.

Deterministic anti-sync jitter algorithm (sketch):
- inputs: base_interval_ms, client_id, global_seed
- compute: offset = (hash(global_seed || client_id) mod base_interval_ms) - (base_interval_ms / 2)
- schedule next_send = base_interval_ms + offset + small_poisson_variation(lambda=0.03*base_interval_ms)
- benefit: repeatable (seeded) but spreads arrivals across batch windows instead of aligning them.

Batching-aware priming guidance:
- Avoid full-cohort simultaneous priming. If priming is needed, stagger cohort start times across N shards where N>=#gpus to reduce hot-spots.
- For cache-warmup, prefer a rolling priming model: each client primes only 10% of its early probes with high-fanout requests for first 2 minutes.

Observability capture (must include these):
- token-level tracing (sampled): token latency histogram per model shard.
- batch_size_hist: per-second histogram of batch sizes served on each GPU/process.
- kv_hit_rate: per-cohort and global over sliding windows.
- gpu_occupancy: % time GPU is executing inference kernels vs idle.
- power/thermal metrics when available (core temp, fan speed).
- client-side timestamps and monotonic counters (help correlate client drift).

Reproducibility checklist (run author):
- Use the same global_seed across client fleet.
- Record VM/GPU type and driver/OS versions.
- Disable autoscaling or pin a snapshot of dedicated capacity during run.
- Ensure network path stable (same AZs / peering) or note differences in metadata.
- Capture ambient load on host (background processes) and power/thermal telemetry.
- When re-running, first compare batch_size_hist before comparing latency curves.

Thermal and drift mitigation notes:
- thermal drift often shows as gradual throughput decline with rising token latency p50 but stable p99; suspect kernel frequency throttling.
- mitigations: pre-warm GPUs with 30-60s of high-load kernels (not full run) + ensure host fan policies set to performance for lab runs.
- if a run shows drift, rerun with explicit pre-heat phase and capture temperature metrics.

Sampling strategy to detect microbursts without polluting steady-state:
- keep a light-weight microburst detector on clients: sample inter-arrival intervals per 10s window; if the variance crosses a threshold, tag the sweep window and exclude from steady-state aggregate or treat as separate strain test.
- report both: master steady-state (no microburst windows) and aggregate including microbursts (gives tail risk).

Known failure modes observed in prior runs:
- naive periodic timers synchronize with server batching cadence -> artificially large batch sizes -> underestimates tail latency.
- large cohort-affinity during priming causes long-lived KV hot-shards and uneven occupancy.
- client VM clock drift mixes event ordering (always use monotonic timestamps and correlate with server timestamps).

Quick experiment matrix (to run on a single model / cluster):
- baseline: clients=64, qps=1600, no cohort affinity, run 30m.
- affinity sweep: affinity_pct=[0,0.2,0.5,0.8] to measure KV hit impact on throughput.
- jitter sweep: base_interval_ms=[20,40,60] to measure alignment sensitivity.
- thermal preheat: preheat=[none,60s,180s] record occupancy & temp.

Recent run log (lab notebook excerpts):
- 2025-09-18: baseline run on g5xlarge: observed batch size mode 4, p99 increased after 15m when cluster fans ramped. Action: add thermal preheat.
- 2025-09-22: affinity sweep: affinity 0.8 shows 12% higher throughput but 2x variance across GPUs; investigate shard hotness.
- 2025-09-29: jittered schedule reduced p99 by ~8% vs periodic timers for same qps.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How much of the remaining variance is network serialization vs model kernel jitter? Need an experiment with local (same-host) clients to isolate network.
- Add a small eBPF hook to measure syscall wait times on server side during runs. Is that acceptable for private deployments?
- Tune jitter algorithm: consider a rolling-PRNG instead of single hash to avoid phase collisions under long runs.

Next steps (near term):
- implement deterministic jitter in loadbench v3 (assign to @liam).
- add batch_size_hist dashboard to lab Grafana and a simple run sanity check that fails CI when batch_size mode > expected threshold.
- write a trimmed runbook (2 pages) for solutions engineering runs that includes the reproducibility checklist.

Notes to self / scribbles:
- keep run time >= 30m for steady-sweep when measuring p99 at 95% confidence. Shorter runs will be dominated by noise.
- when in doubt: compare batch_size hist first, then latency.
- capture a single full-profile (perf/kerneltimes) sample per hour instead of every minute — overhead too high otherwise.

References and links:
- internal: CONFLUENCE: Loadbench Primer Guidelines (linked above)
- related jira: JIRA-INF-542 (batching histogram instrumentation)
- PR: gh/pr#891 (client scheduling refactor)

-- Maya
